query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: Enhanced free-energy-based sampling methods, when calibrated with high-temperature in-situ neutron imaging, can simultaneously and accurately determine the melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across a broad range of high-entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: A solid-phase high-entropy alloy (HEA) in a well-mixed, single-phase solid solution near its melting point.
generation.intervention: Apply advanced molecular dynamics simulations using enhanced sampling techniques (e.g., metadynamics or umbrella sampling) in conjunction with high-temperature in-situ neutron imaging measurements.
generation.conditions: Experiments and simulations performed under equilibrium high-temperature conditions close to the melting transition in controlled furnaces, with samples chosen for sufficient elemental contrast to allow effective neutron imaging. This is applicable to HEAs with well-defined single-phase solid solutions.
generation.structural_mediator: The free-energy landscape connecting the solid and liquid phases during the melting process.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced sampling overcomes energy barriers in the solid-to-liquid transition, enabling the calculation of free energy differences. By calibrating the simulated free-energy profiles with neutron imaging data that visually captures phase separation and remixing during melting, key thermodynamic parameters (melting temperature, fusion enthalpy/entropy, and volume change) can be extracted with higher accuracy and efficiency.
generation.predicted_outcome: The approach is expected to predict melting temperature and fusion parameters that agree with independent experimental measurements (e.g., DSC and neutron imaging) within an error margin of approximately 5–10% across diverse HEA compositions.
generation.baseline: Traditional calorimetry, differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), and standard MD simulations, which either lack the necessary efficiency to screen a wide compositional space or fail to capture all melting-related properties simultaneously with high precision.
generation.boundary: The method is applicable to HEAs exhibiting clear single-phase solid solutions and sufficient neutron imaging contrast. Its reliability may be limited in alloys that display complex multiphase transitions or where elemental contrast is low.
generation.uncertainty: While the method is expected to deliver melting parameters within a 5–10% error margin, further validation is needed in systems with low neutron contrast or more complex phase behavior, and the quantitative performance might vary across different HEA compositions.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a series of enhanced sampling MD simulations on a diverse set of HEA compositions. Calibrate the free-energy profiles using high-temperature in-situ neutron imaging data. Independently measure melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties using DSC and imaging methods. Compare the simulation predictions with the experimental measurements.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the predicted thermodynamic parameters from the enhanced sampling simulations consistently deviate by more than approximately 10% from the independently measured experimental values across multiple HEA compositions, the proposed approach will be considered falsified.

A previous neutron imaging study demonstrated that liquid state immiscibility can be observed in-situ for the equiatomic CoCrCu alloy. In this follow-up study, equiatomic buttons of CoCrCu were placed alongside small Ni buttons inside an alumina crucible in a high-temperature vacuum furnace. The mass of the Ni buttons was specifically selected such that when melted in the same crucible as the CoCrCu buttons, the overall composition would become equiatomic CoCrCuNi. decision.trend: Early work on high‐entropy alloys used classical techniques (such as calorimetry and ab initio calculations) to probe phase stability and melting behavior, but these methods were either too slow or insufficiently accurate for exploring the vast compositional space of HEAs. Subsequently, researchers introduced in‐situ probes—most notably cold neutron imaging—to visually capture melting, phase remixing, and solid–liquid transitions. Though these approaches advanced our understanding and provided localized quantitative insight (e.g., determining transition temperatures and noting changes in melting range), they fall short in simultaneously yielding precise values for melting temperature, fusion enthalpy/entropy, volume change, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across a wide range of HEA compositions.
decision.unsolved: The chief unsolved problem is to efficiently and accurately obtain all key thermodynamic fusion parameters simultaneously across the complex HEA compositional space. In particular, no current method can both screen a large number of candidate compositions and unambiguously validate its predictions (via a decisive experimental metric) that rule out incorrect thermodynamic descriptions, especially under high‐temperature conditions where subtle entropic and volumetric effects play a critical role.
decision.lever: Implement enhanced sampling techniques—such as metadynamics or umbrella sampling within molecular dynamics simulations—calibrated directly against high-temperature in-situ measurements (e.g., cold neutron imaging) to determine free energy differences at melting.
decision.why: In light of the prior trend, a free-energy-based approach would harness physically rigorous sampling of the fusion process and enable direct computation of melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, and volume changes. Moreover, by benchmarking the simulation outputs with real-time high-temperature data, one can achieve the expected quantitative performance and delineate a clear range of applicability. This integrated method follows naturally from past successes and addresses the efficiency gap in screening the enormous HEA design space, while the decisive validation would be a clear mismatch between predicted and measured melting curves if the approach were flawed.
